The Pixel 9 XL Pro by Google has impressed me. A 6.8" display in a beautiful, slick body that doesn't feel overly large in the hands, but I would have liked a slightly smaller 6.6” screen. I'm so happy Google went completely flat screen and bezels. I never liked curved screens. It feels solid and well-built. It has a heft this year that makes it feel high quality. The curved edges of the body only enhance its looks and help make it more comfortable in the hands. The rear camera module has changed from the Pixel 6, 7, and 8 but maintains a distinctly Pixel look. The polished metal frame feels solid and adds a touch of sophistication. Pixel 9 Pro XL feels grown up to steal The refreshed design with a pill-shaped camera bar looks sleek and one of a kind in the current bar phone market. The Pixel 7 and 8 were great-looking phones and very unique but the Pixel 9 Pro looks better in every way. This is the best-looking phone that Google has made (although the Pixel 4 Panda color scheme is a pretty close second or tied)

The screen is beautiful with the highest brightness on a cell phone at 3000 nits. I did not have an issue with visibility in bright sunlight. The bezels seem more uniform and slimmer this year. The OLED screen appears to extend to the edges. The flattened frame means you won’t accidentally tap the edges of the display, either. The Pixel Pro’s upgraded panel is called Super Actua - which is marketing but it frankly is the best screen Google has put on a phone. The screen is vibrant, sharp, and immersive. It's super responsive and the one to 120Hz refresh rate makes everything glide. There are times when the animations are fast but not necessarily smooth but everything has been fluid in my usage.

This year the Pixel Pro comes with 16GB of RAM. According to reports, 13GB is for the operating system, and 3GB to be used for the Gemini AI. While the raw performance of the Tensor G4 may not be the main focus, its software capabilities are what set it apart. The benchmark results of the chip against the flagship competition exhibit expected results. The Tensor G4 is slower and runs throttles more than its rivals. Pixel fans will have to wait until next year, as we’re expected to see a raw power boost while being built at TMSC’s factories. But not to worry, the raw power of the phone and chipset will not hurt the overall experience. Most users won't push the CPU or GPU to their limits. I haven’t noticed much of a difference compared to my previous device. Users should be more than happy with the phone as it keeps pace with the average person’s needs.

As far as battery life, I can’t complain. The phone lasts 5+ hours of on-screen time before the need to charge. I've seen and heard a lot about the fast charging capabilities of the phone, but I find that the phone charges quickly enough. How many people need to charge from zero to 100 in 30 minutes? Most people I know are charging throughout the day. 27 watts on the Pixel 9 Pro XL while connected to a USB-C adapter I already owned is pretty fast, but more importantly, it's fast enough.


The Pixel 9 Pro camera delivers everything you expect from a flagship device. The camera opens fast and loads fast and it focuses within milliseconds. Those factors are almost as important as quality photos. I have owned phones that were expensive but didn't focus quickly or well. Its performance in low light is outstanding, and it excels in daylight, with good macro shots. It's probably the best point-and-click camera on a phone. 

The big push this year is the features powered by Google’s Gemini AI.  Google is giving you one year of Gemini Advanced. Gemini Assistant is the built-in AI assistant. I find it can handle complex queries and tasks better than Google Assistant, especially considering all the intelligence and features they've taken away from Google Assistant. Then you have the Photography Enhancements like Magic Editor, Auto Frame, Add Me, Pixel Studio, and the new Pixel Weather app. I used them all and used them on almost a daily basis…so far. I find them useful and some of the photo AI features are just fun. Reimagine lets you recreate the selected area of an image based on a written prompt. It's far from perfect but I've had a lot of fun coming up with new backgrounds to my family photos.

I could talk for pages on the different AI features and how well they work or how rough around the edges they are but I appreciate the direction Google is taking the Pixel line. The features are also far ahead of what other manufacturers offer on their devices. AI is the future and Google has been doing this for years. I hope they keep implementing AI in ways that make things easier from your phone and just make life easier. Google has been very good at pushing features to the Pixels for the last few years. I expect them to improve AI features, Gemini, and Android. I am disappointed that Android 15 wasn't onboard from day one but we're supposed to get it soon. The Pixel 9 Pro XL offers several compelling reasons to consider it for your next smartphone purchase. If you’re looking for a smartphone that combines cutting-edge AI features, exceptional camera performance, and a refined design, the Pixel 9 Pro XL is a terrific choice.

Pixel 7 Pro, What You Need To Know. The Pixel 7 Pro is the latest flagship phone from Google. After using this phone for 8 months here are my thoughts.

Pros: 

-Cameras. The absolute best point and shoot smartphone camera you can get. I've used pretty much every phone and you won't get better photos than this. Just try to take a photo of a pet or one of your kids moving around and you will see the difference! This year they've added a 5x optical zoom lens that zooms in up to 30x as well as a macro camera mode. I love using both of these modes and you only get them on the 7 Pro and not the regular 7.

- Android as Google intended it. Absolutely no bloatware on this phone like you get with some other companies(Samsung I'm looking at you!). You also get updates to Android as soon as they are released. 

- Connectivity. I have no issues picking up signal around town. This was an issue with the 6 series and Google upgraded to a new modem for the 7 series that fixed the connectivity issues.

Cons:

- Tensor G2. Tensor went to Samsung to make their processors for the Pixel line and they just aren't up to the level of the latest Snapdragon flagship chips like the 8 Gen 2. 

- Thermals. This phone gets hot! It generally stays warm when doing anything on it, but it feels on fire if you try to use it while it's charging.

- Charging speeds. Charging is capped at 23 watts. This is really slow in 2023 when compared to the latest Samsung S23 Ultra that can charge at 45 watts or the OnePlus 11 that can charge at 100 watts.

Overall I stick with the Google Pixel as my main phone thanks to stock Android with no bloat and the amazing cameras that are unbeatable, but I'm really hoping the Tensor G3 in the Pixel 8 Pro is a large improvement for processor efficiency that can compete more with the latest and greatest from Snapdragon.

Camera Excellence: The Pixel’s camera lives up to the hype! From low-light magic to high-definition detail, I’ve captured some truly professional-looking photos. The computational photography is next-level, and the Night Sight mode still blows my mind.

Pure Google Experience: Having the latest Android updates straight from Google has been fantastic. It’s bloat-free and smooth, and the customizations just keep getting better. The Pixel’s exclusive features, like “Hold for Me” and “Call Screen,” make daily life simpler and more efficient.

Battery Life and Charging: The battery has stayed consistent throughout the year. I get a full day without the dreaded mid-afternoon “low battery” warning, and the charging speed is reliable and quick.

Performance and Speed: No signs of slowing down! With apps, multitasking, and gaming, it’s always responsive. The integration with Google Assistant is seamless and genuinely useful – I find myself using it more than ever.

A Few Minor Quirks: No device is perfect, and the Pixel does have minor quirks. Occasionally, I’ve noticed a slight lag in the camera app. And while I love the sleek design, it’s a bit slippery, so a case is a must!

Verdict: For anyone wanting a streamlined Android experience, a standout camera, and a smart, reliable device, I highly recommend the Pixel. It’s a year in, and I’d still choose it again in a heartbeat!

The Next Step in Google Tesor G2. I’ve always preferred Google Pixel phones over the competition. There are several reasons. The first is that it is the cleanest form of Android without all the bloatware tacked on. This is especially true when you compare it to the biggest Android device manufacturer in the world. The second is because the software experience, with its Pixel-exclusive features, that give these phones the edge over the competition. And lastly, the camera processing. Google has been the leader in handling image processing for several years. And while the rest of the competition has finally caught up, Google manages to find little things that sets it apart from the rest.

For the first time, and because of the age of the previous phone, I decided to directly transfer my apps and data to the Pixel 7 Pro. The process is simple and brings the majority of data over. And thankfully, an app that I use to keep track of work punches retains the data that I have on the old phone. Once all that data is transferred over, I let the phone download and reinstall the 3rd party apps. Sadly, all my Bluetooth devices that were connected to the old phone did not transfer over. So I have to set all those back up once again.

The software experience is great as anticipated. And since all my preferences and customizations were transferred over, I did not have to redo all my icon placements and organization. While I’d like to give the phone some more time to check for more quirks and small issues, I simply cannot find anything wrong with Android as a whole. Perhaps this is just due to having used Android for so long.

Older Pixel users will be paying attention to this section, as it pertains to biometric security. When I used the Pixel 6a, I initially had some issues with the under-display fingerprint reader. And while software updates did eventually resolve most of this, it was not the best first impression experience. It was of great concern due to my workplace, which involves handling boxes and books for several hours. So I came in hoping the Pixel 7 Pro would provide a better first impression experience. And thus far, it’s working. But as lessons learned, I opted to utilize all four fingerprint registration slots for both thumbs for the best possible outcome. It’s not the fastest optical print reader. But it’s an improvement over the previous phones. Added to the Pixel 7 series is face unlock, which makes a strange return but using just the camera and AI/ML to recognize the face. As a security conscious person, I did not use this.

Charging the phone up can be done via USB-C or wirelessly. It supports up to 23w charging in either mode but wireless charging comes with a caveat. That fast wireless charging only comes if you use Google’s proprietary charger. Otherwise, you’re limited to 12w according to Google. While this is disappointing to limit the speed of wireless charging when not using Google’s own charger, most people probably would not mind as much since it will be charged overnight while we sleep.

The display is a new experience for me. It is my first high refresh display phone. Initially, I could not tell the difference. But after some speed scrolling, I started to notice the difference. High speed scrolling and fast animation really looks smoother when the refresh rate is cranked up high. And such a thing is slowly growing on me. There is concern for power consumption. But so far, it has lasted all day for me for medium use. I do have a couple of issues with the display. One of which is minor and is probably fixable using software. The other, though, is an issue by design. The display is curved very slightly on the edges, which makes finding an affordable screen protector that properly covers the entire displayed area difficult. I very much prefer a display that is all flat with no curved area at all. Honestly, all future phones need to go back to a flat glass altogether so we don’t have to worry about keeping our protectors in the center and straight. But that’s a different matter altogether.

Other hardware performance seems pretty good so far. Just like the software, I did not run into any hardware issue. The WiFi is 6E capable but I have no router to test this with. Even WiFi 5 spec is fast enough for most tasks. I still wish there is a headphone jack for times when I go into crowded areas and there are a lot of wireless signals (ie. riding the train).

Camera performance has been great. I did not bother taking daytime shots since almost any phone camera can take decent daytime photos. Instead, I focused on other aspects such as night shots, astrophotography, and macro shots. And the Pixel 7 Pro delivers on that. Macro photography can be a bit tricky, since it switches to a different camera module to take the photo. I don’t know if this is something that’s desirable. But with enough light, the image can turn out good. Astrophotography is wonderful, but only if you have a tripod to mount the phone on.

Cell network connectivity is nice but trying to test mmWave isn’t feasible. With no way to find out where a mmWave area is, I cannot see for myself just how fast this tech is. But other 5G bands work when available.

As a whole, the Pixel 7 Pro is a great phone for those who want that stock Android and Pixel experience. There are some weird quirks, such as wireless charging being limited to 12w max. Swiping is a bit odd and I am not sure if this is due to the 120Hz refresh rate or if this is software related. Either you need to swipe a longer distance to get the desired scrolling effect or it will either not work or scroll very little. The slightly curved display edges don't sit well with me and I prefer a totally flat screen or glass altogether. If you can look past these, then it’s a great phone to get. However, is it worth the MSRP? It’s a tough call. On the hardware end, you’re getting a 5x telephoto camera module, a 120Hz refresh rate display, more RAM, a larger phone which equates to larger battery and screen, and a higher resolution. If you’re able to afford it, then by all means it’s a good buy. But if you’re concerned more about the value of the phone you’re getting, it’s probably better to either get the smaller sibling or try to get this phone at a discount, either on sale or via trade in.

Verdict: Buy if discounted

Pixel 6 Pro, Refined. I’ve been on the Google phone train going back to the Nexus days. In the beginning it was about getting the pure, unbloated Google experience with fast software updates. I’ve always just sort of accepted that I would never have the ‘best’ phone, but I would have the best experience. The Pixel 6 Pro last year felt like it was finally going to be the phone to have both, but some rough edges and bugginess that came a bit after its release put a damper on the ‘experience’ part. Software updates improved things a bit, but it feels like Google really went in and fixed everything with the Pixel 7 Pro. It feels a lot like the phone that maybe should have come out last year and while not everything is perfect, the Pixel 7 Pro is still a fantastic phone and a great value if you’re looking for a high-but-not-quite-highest end Google experience.

Getting the phone unboxed I immediately noticed the difference in build quality. The 6 Pro wasn’t a badly built phone by any means, but it had some funky bits like the bolted-on camera bar and large plastic antenna bar. The 7 Pro changes the glass camera bar to aluminum and seamlessly blends the camera part into the frame of the phone. I’ve seen reviews where that aluminum bar seems to scratch easily though and will be keeping mine in its case 99% of the time to avoid that. The antenna cutout at the top is significantly reduced and it’s a lot less noticeable now. The screen is still curved, which is not my favorite, but the curve has been reduced and is not so aggressive on the 7 Pro. The buttons feel as good as ever and have been lowered slightly from the 6 Pro so they’re easier to reach now.

Setup was straightforward. I transferred everything over from my Pixel 6 Pro via USB and was up and running in under an hour. One thing I’ve always enjoyed about Google phones is they don’t load them up with bloat and I can happily say that is the case here as well. Carrier versions may preload a couple carrier apps like MyVerizon, but those are easy to remove if you don’t use them. Android 13 isn’t a huge change over Android 12 from last year, but it’s had the benefit of time to sort out all of Android 12’s associate bugs. So far I can’t recall encountering any bugs with the 7 Pro, at least none that have stuck in my mind. I’ll be keep my eye on this though as the experience with my 6 Pro was initially very good and it wasn’t until a month or so later when the bugs really set in.

Performance so far has been excellent on the 7 Pro. The Tensor G2 isn’t the highest end processor you can get on an Android phone, but I couldn’t really tell from my usage. Everything loads quickly and all the animations are very snappy. I’ve also noticed a big improvement with image processing on the camera. It’s not a huge jump over the original Tensor from last year, but I don’t think it really needed to be. Wireless connectivity is also much improved this time around. It was never an outright hindrance for me on the 6 Pro, but I’ve definitely noticed stronger cellular signals. The screen is a 6.7” 120Hz OLED like last year and looks great. Supposedly it does get brighter than the 6 Pro, but in general it looks fairly similar. Screen resolution is QHD, but out of the box it’s set to FHD. I assume this is for battery reasons, but I went ahead and set mine to full resolution and so far I am not regretting that decision. The 7 Pro has a similar stereo speaker setup to last year’s Pixel and they sound good for both calls and watching videos.

The fingerprint reader on the 6 Pro was definitely my biggest gripe with that phone. It was just far too inconsistent for me and I never felt like I could trust I’d get my phone unlocked on the first try. Unfortunately I can’t say if the fingerprint reader on the 7 Pro is that much better, but Google added face unlock this year and that’s helped the general usability for me a lot. Face unlock uses the front camera and there’s no special IR hardware involved. It works really well in good lighting, but tends to fall apart as soon as the lights dim. I would classify as ‘okay’ along with the fingerprint reader, but the nice thing is you can use both together and typically when one of them misses, the other one hits, so despite neither of them being great, together it creates a much better unlocking situation.

The main camera has the same sensor, but Google brought improvements to the ultrawide and telephoto lenses and added some extra software tricks to make it even better. The 50MP camera now has a trick similar to what Apple has done on the new iPhones that lets you do a 2x zoom using just the center portion of the image sensor. This effectively gives you a native 2x zoom, albeit using smaller pixels. They’ve done the same thing with the now 5x telephoto, so with 3 cameras you now have an ultrawide, 1x, 2x, 5x, and 10x zooms with no digital upsampling. The ultrawide camera also gets a macro mode, which is pretty cool. Photos from the main camera still look the best of the 3, but I’ve gotten pictures from each of the lenses at multiple zoom levels that I’m really happy with. Pictures still have that signature very contrasty Pixel look that sometimes feels just a tad over processed and I do wish there was a way to back that off just a bit. The video quality has also improved and you can now record in 10-bit HDR, which looks great, but is limited to 30fps. I do wish Google’s camera app had a 24fps selection for video for a more cinematic look.

The battery life so far for me has not been top class, but still very good. Starting at 4am and ending around 9pm-10pm I’m usually at 30-40%. It’s not quite the full 2-day experience that I’ve been able to get with my iPhone 13 Pro Max, but it’s nothing I’m ever concerned about.

In the week I’ve spent with the Pixel 7 Pro, I’ve often forgotten I’m not carrying my 6 Pro around anymore, but the subtle improvements have added up to an overall much better experience for me. If you already have the 6 Pro I don’t necessarily think you need to rush out and upgrade, but if you were wary of jumping on the Pixel train last year because of all the software issues so far I can say they appear to be a thing of the past. I still recommend the Pixel series to anybody looking for an Android phone and the Pixel 7 Pro hasn’t given me any reason to change my mind.

Disappointing Experience. I had high hopes for the Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra, but unfortunately, it has been a major letdown. Despite all the hype and premium pricing, the phone falls short in several key areas.

First, the performance is surprisingly inconsistent. For a flagship device, I expected smooth multitasking and lightning-fast app launches, but instead, I’ve experienced frequent lagging and occasional crashes. It's simply not what you expect from a phone that’s supposed to represent the cutting edge of Android technology.

Battery life is another huge disappointment. Even with moderate use, I find myself scrambling for a charger halfway through the day. For a phone that's advertised to have an all-day battery, this is unacceptable.

The camera — usually Samsung’s strong suit — also misses the mark. Photos often come out over-processed and lack the natural sharpness and color accuracy I was hoping for. Night mode struggles with clarity, and zoomed-in shots are almost unusable.

Design-wise, while it looks premium at first glance, the phone is surprisingly uncomfortable to hold for long periods, and it feels bulkier than it needs to be. The software doesn't help either; One UI feels bloated, with a lot of unnecessary features that slow the phone down rather than enhance the experience.

Overall, the Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra feels like a rushed, overpriced product that doesn't live up to its promises. I expected a top-tier experience and instead got frustration. Definitely not worth the upgrade.

The display is still beautiful and performance for daily tasks was smooth and reliable.

The Areas for Improvement: Over the last few months, I did notice the battery life starting to fade. It began to struggle to get through a full heavy day on a single charge, which was a primary reason for my upgrade. Also, the 128GB of storage started to feel a bit tight, especially with all the high-resolution photos and videos.

Conclusion: Overall, the Pixel 9 Pro XL was a fantastic phone. If you're looking for a device with a world-class camera and a pure Android experience and can find it at a good price, it's still a very capable option in 2025. For me, the improved battery and performance on the new model made the upgrade worth it.

A Lotta For the Buck. My overall thoughts on the Moto G Stylus (2024) is that it's a good midrange phone (and an absolute steal when it's sold at $250). The leather back makes the phone feel more premium than it is and it comes with a slew of nice features that most higher end phones don't, like the SD card slot and headphone jack. 

I also think this phone has a nice mixture of software and hardware. On the software side, the custom Moto skin offers a lot of nice features including gestures to trigger the flashlight or camera and a desktop like tool called Smart Connect to offer a more desktop like experience that you can use on an external monitor. On the hardware side, you get a big and good looking display, the advertised stylus (which feels surprisingly premium), and an overall solid feeling device.

The only gripes I have with this phone is that the software can be buggy at times (an examples includes the weather widget that comes installed on the phone not displaying correctly when you first turn your phone on) and the phone is set to only get one major Android upgrade. The stylus is also not the most responsive, especially if you're using a screen protector.

With that being said, I would recommend the Moto G Stylus to anyone looking for a phone that offers a lot of bang for your buck.

Best Take gives you the ability to swap out closed eyelids or silly faces for perfect shots using other images of those people.

Other photo features: You can move subjects in a photo around in the image. You can use AI to add in flying pigs or whatever your heart desires. And you can edit out undesirable things like random people or objects you just don't want in your photo.

While taking photos the AI detects persons in the image and gives you best suggestions verbally about framing and shooting the image to result in the best picture possible.

I've been using the Samsung Galaxy A16 5G for a bit now, and for a budget phone, it's been a pleasant surprise. I also appreciate Samsung's promise of six years of updates, which makes me feel confident this phone will stay useful for longer than most budget devices.

Performance is smooth for everyday stuff like texting, browsing, and streaming. If I load up too many apps at once it can stutter a little, but closing a couple brings things right back to normal—so in practice it's easy to manage. The 50 MP main camera takes sharp photos in good light, while the extra lenses are fine for casual shots; video tops out at 1080p, which is good enough for social posts and family clips.

One important note: the A16 5G does not include Samsung's Galaxy AI features (those live AI tools are reserved for higher-end models). For me that wasn't a dealbreaker—if Galaxy AI is essential, you'll want to look up the midrange or flagship options. Overall, the A16 5G is reliable, long-lasting, and a great everyday phone for the price.

Great phone - subtle yet exciting improvements. There's a lot to like about the Google Pixel 9 and I have been a fan of the Pixel phones since the Pixel 5.  There are moderate improvements in the Pixel 9.

Physically the phone is slightly larger in every dimension than the Pixel 8 (by 1-2mm L/W/D) and slightly heavier (by 10g).   This doesn't sound like much, but I found it to feel noticeably larger in my hand and pocket.  

Setup was very easy with the setup wizard and all my apps and setting transferred over effortlessly. 
 
With the Tensor 4 processor and 12GB of onboard RAM everything is smooth, smooth, smooth!  I have some apps that on other phones seemed a bit laggy or glitchy, but on the Pixel 9 I don't notice anything of the sort.  The screen is nice and bright and the adaptive brightness works surprisingly well.  

Of course, AI is the latest fad for all things electronic and the Google Gemini AI works well without being overbearing or obtrusive, but I have not used it to the full potential.

As a photographer and specifically an astrophotographer who regularly shoots in low light situations, I think where the Pixel 9 differentiates itself is in the camera and in low light situations.  Taking video in a moderately dim basement living space, there is a HUGE improvement in the clarity and colors of video.  Think SD vs HD quality.  I was honestly shocked by this improvement.  Low light video is much sharper and far less grainy.  I didn't have a chance to try the camera for night time photography, but I am excited to see how the camera performs for things like the Milky Way and northern lights with the long exposure feature.  

The only negative I would point to is the battery life does not seem as robust as compared to the Pixel 8, by about 20% over a 12 hour span.

Honest Review From Someone Who Loves a Good Phone. Alright, so I’ve had the S25 Ultra for a little while now, and just being real—it’s kind of a beast.

First off, the screen is crazy good. I didn’t think I’d care that much, but once I started using it, I totally got the hype. Super smooth scrolling, bright even outside, and the colors are sharp without looking fake. Watching anything on this phone just hits different.

The camera is honestly one of my favorite parts. I’m not a professional or anything, but I’ve taken some pictures that look like I actually know what I’m doing. The zoom? Ridiculous. I zoomed in on the moon for fun and it actually looked good. And low light shots don’t come out all grainy like older phones—I was impressed.

Battery life has been solid too. I use my phone a lot—work stuff, texting, YouTube, and way too much scrolling—and it still makes it through the whole day. Now here’s the thing: it charges fast, but only if you use the right charger. It supports 45W charging, but they don’t give you the charger in the box—you just get a USB-C cable. I bought the Samsung 45W charger separately and yeah, it’s worth it. It charges the phone super fast, like 50% in half an hour kind of fast.

Performance-wise, no issues. It’s fast, smooth, handles everything I throw at it—games, apps, switching between stuff—it all just works without lag.

Now let me be honest about the S Pen. I don’t really use it. I thought I might, but it just kinda sits there. And when you get a case, there’s this weird little cutout on the bottom corner for the S Pen, and it kinda messes with the whole clean look of the phone. Personally? I hope Samsung drops the S Pen next time and focuses more on battery or trimming the size a bit.

Speaking of size—yeah, it’s a big phone. Like, it’s not something you one-hand easily. But after a few days, I got used to it, and honestly the big screen is worth it.

Overall? Yeah, it’s expensive. But if you’re someone who actually uses their phone a lot, this one’s worth every penny. It feels premium, looks amazing, runs like a dream, and it’s one of those phones that makes you excited to use it

The AI features are a pain in the rear to turn off, as there isn't much of a reason to use it since they use so much power. All in all it's a good phone, it's got a ton of useful features, plenty of battery life and good camera; however the cost is prohibitive and not worth stretching yourself to pay.

Samsung ha vuelto a superarse con el panel Dynamic AMOLED, y el brillo, incluso bajo el sol más intenso de mediodía, es increíble. Todo se ve nítido, con colores vibrantes y una fluidez exquisita gracias a la tasa de refresco adaptativa.
Pero hablemos de lo que de verdad importa: el rendimiento y las cámaras. El S25 Ultra viene con el nuevo chip Snapdragon 8 Elite for Galaxy, y vaya que se nota. Todo vuela. No hay aplicación, por pesada que sea, que lo haga titubear. La multitarea es una gozada y los juegos más exigentes corren con una suavidad y unos gráficos que no había visto en un móvil. Coming from Android. Unboxing: nothing special here the box contains the phone, a charger, sim removal tool, charging cable, wired headphones.

Set up:
Coming from a Flagship Android device I thought it would be a very tough task to transfer data from my Android to this Iphone SE second edition. I was wrong!
once I started the iphone it asked me if I want to get my data from another device and gave me the option of transfer from Android. 
asked me to download an app called MOVE TO IOS. I downloaded the app and then followed the instructions and the transfer started wirelessly and took about an hour or so.

I restarted the phone, created an Apple ID, added my fingerprint, and went about to install my apps and import my Google accounts, and downloaded the latest IOS updates.
Restarted the phone again and started using the phone.

Experience:
The phone is very snappy and fast, although you will notice some tracing while scrolling menus due to the lower refresh rate but the phone performs very very well and I can say that with this price point, nothing can beat this hardware and software Experience:
The IPhone SE 2 has the latest A13 Bionec Chip, an OK screen size and quality, and a very nice camera compared to other phones in this price range.

Build Quality and design:
The build quality is solid. it took me less than 3 hours to drop the phone from the table on hardwood floor flat on its screen. I thought the screen was shattered. I was wrong again.
the design is very similar to the IPhone 8 with its rounded edges and the silver frame with a glass front and back. 
although when tapping on the screen with my finger nails, it feels more plastic than glass compared to my other phones.
the power button is located on the right side, and the volume rockers are located on the left side.
this phone does not have stereo jack and instead uses a lightning port (Thanks Apple!), and dual stereo speakers at the button of the phone.
this phone still has a physical button on the left side above the volume rockers to switch to silent mode if you want to. and the sim card slot is located on the right side under the power button.
the finger print touch is located in the center of the screen at the buttom.
the phone has a double chin that measures about a half inch at the top and buttom. and the screen size is 4.7 inches (usable but would love bigger one for sure).
The phone is perfectly balanced and feels good in your hand even if you have a smaller hand. it doesn't feel lightweight and cheap but it doesnt feel and look like a flagship either. 
the frame of the phone is made of metal.
the camera has a slight bump, and has a single camera on the back with a sensor and a flash. the camera app has Portrait, panoramic, slowmo, time- lapse, video, photo out of the box.
you can change the quality and size of the photos and videos and you can record videos of up to 4K with 60 frames per seconds which will cost you a hefty 400MG per minute of recording.
after setting up and importing the necessities from my other phone I was left with less than 20 GB of the 64GB this phone comes with. not much considering i am just done with setup and havent actually used the phone yet. but you can always upgrade to the 128 GB version of this phone. 
Battery life:
after using the phone with everything on out of the box I was able to get about 9 hours of continuous use and wast still left with 37% battery life. not bad considering that the phone has wireless charging capability and comes with a fast charging cable (but not a fast charger!). 
Sound quality:
the sound quality of this phone is OK, not great but its just good. the same goes for the included wired headphones. you can use them for sure, but we all know you are going to upgrade to those nice wireless pro's.

final thoughts:
The IPhone SE 2 is a great cheap smart phone in the $400 range for any IOS or Android user. 
the A13 Bionec chip is the latest and fastest IOS chip to date, its the same chip used in the flagship Iphone today. 
the smaller screen with the less refresh rate and the older looking design are not deal breakers considering you are getting the same flawless experience from Apple.
I switched from Android to Apple for a few reasons:
1- there are apps I need for work that are not available for Android (these are custom made Apps that I need in my day to day work)
2- Security features: although Android has great customization capabilities, but security is still and issue. Apple is superior when it comes to protecting your privacy and security.
3- Some gimmick features that I see everyone around me love and use like Facetime, and impressions in Imessage.

finally, I would totally recommend this phone for anyone who wants to buy an affordable phone with great features and support that will last at least 3 years from Apple. this phone is also a great entry to IOS for anyone coming from Android family.

Last point: if you are an Android user and want to make the switch but afraid that your most valuable apps wont work, rest assured that everything from Google is available on the apple store even Google Authenticator. if you are missing some of Apple features with Android, you can make this leap of faith and will be happy with this purchase.

The Galaxy A16 5G is a budget-friendly 5G smartphone that delivers a solid user experience with a few standout features. Its 6.5-inch Super AMOLED display offers vibrant colors and deep contrasts, making media consumption enjoyable. While the 90Hz refresh rate isn't the highest, it ensures smooth scrolling and seamless actions across apps.  

Performance is handled by a modest chipset, which handles daily tasks well but may struggle with intensive gaming. The 5G connectivity future-proofs the device, providing fast downloads and low latency where available. The 5,000mAh battery easily lasts a full day, though charging speeds are average.  

The triple-camera setup includes a 50MP main sensor, capturing decent photos in good lighting but struggling in low light. The 2MP macro and depth sensors feel like filler additions. The 13MP front camera is adequate for selfies and video calls. One notable software feature is the audio eraser tool, which helps minimize background noise in recordings—a handy addition for content creators.  

The plastic build keeps the phone lightweight, though it lacks premium feel. The side-mounted fingerprint sensor is fast and reliable. Running One UI over Android, the software is feature-rich but occasionally bloated.  

Overall, the Galaxy A16 5G is a good budget option for those prioritizing display quality, battery life, and 5G, but performance and camera capabilities are just average.

Google Pixel 7 Pro - Revenge of the Pixel. To set things up, I will say that I owned a Pixel 4 XL and that I absolutely LOVED it. So much that I didn't upgrade until two years later. I have run with the other major competitor's products as it was more affordable at the time. But when I first saw the release announcement for the Pixel 7, I was stoked and declared to the mighty gods of technology that I would own one. I do now and it's awesome.

I'm not going to list all the specs, but highlight some that really stick out.

The Pixel 7 Pro is armed with a Google custom made processor in it's second generation. The Tensor 2 as it is called, is more powerful than its first iteration and that's saying something. It's a more mature version of the Tensor and quite an upgrade from the previous model. The Pixel 7 harnesses the power of this processor very well as it provides enough "oomph" for everything you like to do. The screen has a nice vibrant and crisp image. It's a 6.7" QHD+ (1440 x 3120) LTPO OLED display which can go up to 120Hz refresh rates. And lets not forget the HDR support and 1,000,000:1 contrast ratio. It sports 12 gigs of brand new DDR5 memory, which is lightning fast. Another innovation is packed into the Pixel 7 which is the support of the new WIFI 6E bands.

The phone itself has a nice feel to it and seems solid. It just looks and feels very refined. Buttons and Type-C ports are easily accessible.

What most amazed me was the quality of the camera(s). I have taken pictures in many different light conditions and with different subjects and the pictures are simply fabulous (thanks to the  50 MP Octa PD Quad Bayer wide camera).

Now to what really matters: the phone's OS. Google has veered off from the regular Android distribution in favor of their own version tailored to the phones' hardware. If you've never had a Google phone, you will very likely find it odd to use and navigate at first, but after just a day or two, you'll realize that everything has been done to allow you to get things done faster. Speaking of faster, there are times when the phone might appear slightly sluggish. I believe that system updates will fix that and more (the Pixel 7 was just released at the time of writing).

I've thrown everything I could think of at it: games, power-hungry apps, videos, streaming, social media and more. The Pixel 7 Pro could handle all of it and then some. The battery at the end of the day wasn't even below 25% of battery. Quite impressive!

The bottom line: The Pixel 7 Pro is a great phone, with plenty of power and good battery life, a sublime screen and a custom Android version which is one of the most intuitive I have had the pleasure to use. Also, the price-tag is low compared to what you would pay for other phones with the same or less features as the Pixel 7 provides. I can only recommend it.

When I finally managed to speak with an agent after numerous attempts, I requested that they pull up the video footage from the time of purchase to prove that I had indeed asked for a warranty. This evidence would be crucial in supporting my claim and ensuring that justice was served.

It is essential for businesses to uphold their responsibilities towards customers by providing accurate information and offering warranties when necessary. As consumers, we place our trust in these establishments and expect them to deliver on their promises.

In conclusion, while it may have taken me over a week to address this issue due to personal commitments, it is imperative that businesses understand the importance of honoring warranties. Solid phone. Motorola is back!. Motorola has finally produced a true flagship again. Having been a big fan back in the day, it's great to see them back in the game after years of mediocrity. I must say this is one of the fastest phones out there, right up there with the more expensive S23 Ultra, and much faster than the Pixel 7 Pro. 

PROS:
+Clean, near stock Android UI with useful add-ons
+Efficient Snapdragon 8 Gen 2 and UFS 4.0 
+165 hz display is very smooth and vibrant
+5100 mAh battery lasts incredibly long
+Solid build quality, metal frame, Gorilla Glass Victus
+Extremely comfortable to hold 
+Back panel is fingerprint resistant
+Pricing is competitive

CONS:
-The curved display is more sloped than the S23 Ultra and Pixel 7 Pro and is somewhat distracting. 
-8 GB of RAM seems a bit light considering the European model has 12 GB RAM
-A true Always On Display would be a nice option
-Cameras are inferior to the S23 Ultra and Pixel 7 Pro

There are a few things that hold this phone back from being samsung or apple level quality. First and foremost, the fingerprint reader is trash. I've never had so many issues with a reader since they were introduced almost the decade ago. I've been locked out of so many accounts. I know some apps require it, as it's the only biometrics that can be used, but if you can, use it as little as possible. Use the facial or pattern unlocks. The second issue is the stock Android interface. Simple thing such as creating folders are non-existent. Be prepared to scroll through pages and pages of apps even before you add your own. Yes, you can download a launcher but that just adds bloat and security issues to your phone to fix a simple issue. You have the ability to make folders just on your homepage and not on your apps pages. Why? The third issue is upgrades. The phone upgrades your system while keeping it fully available to use. In theory, this sounds good, but this translates into a three megabyte update taking hours to complete. A major upgrade could take overnight or longer, Instead of just taking your phone offline for a few minutes like other phones do. You should at least have the option to either keep using the phone or letting the update take priority. If you're not looking to spend a thousand plus dollars for a Samsung and don't want to pay the Apple tax, this phone should be at the top of your list. But if ease of use is at the top of your list, the extra $500 for those other phones may be worth it.

Phone feels great in my hands and laying it flat, its actually fairly stable. With a solid case, this shouldn't really matter anyway.

Regarding the camera itself, Google does not disappoint once again. Photos are crisp and beautiful like any other Pixel phone. The Pixel 7 actually has the same cameras as the Pro minus the 48mp telephoto on the Pro. Nevertheless, the quality of the camera combined with Google's image software will not disappoint you.

The Pixel 7 also comes with Google's new Tensor G2, a very solid processing chip. While not a huge improvement over the previous generation, it allows the Pixel to be smooth and efficient with tons of battery life. So far, battery life for me as last over 24 hours using the Adaptive battery. 

Overall, the Pixel 7 is definitely the best android phone on the market right now, especially considering its price point. You get an amazing camera, solid software and updates (including security updates), and phone that performs smoothly and fast while providing day long battery life. I definitely recommend the Pixel 7 especially if you're just entering the android market.

Its a decent iPhone but should be better. I give it 4 stars depending on what you are upgrading from.  If from something older than a 13 or so then it will be a pretty amazing upgrade.  But there are still a few dated things about this phone that make me give 1 star less.  I feel like Apple is a bit behind the curve at this point.  This phone is still pretty amazing but it could be better.

Design:  Meh I mean there is only so much you can do with an iPhone or any phone but this is dated.  I can't stand the camera bump and how it makes the phone tilt.  If you use your phone careless it's a huge pain.  The titanium is OK, but honestly the thing is far too heavy.  And it got a smidge heavier from the 15 Pro Max, these phones need to lose some weight to be truly comfortable. 

Screen:  Exceptional.  the 120MHz and colors, etc are all great.  Apple needs to work on PWM (flickering) if you are sensitive to it (many are not) its not great, Apple could spring a few bucks to have a great MHz but they have not done so and its cheap in my opinion.  But overall it's a great display.  The 16 Plus should have 120MHz at this point I would have gotten that one if it did.  Again Apple being cheap and not bringing tech that should be in 2024 as a minimum on all devices given what they charge.

A18 Pro:  amazing I mean iOS will not even blink with this chip.  The phone can overheat but so far it's been good compared to my 15Max which was overheating constantly and while annoying would constantly dim the display and that was super annoying when it happened.  So let's hope that is truly taken care of.

Colors:  So boring.  I got the Desert and its nice, its like a Rosy Gold in certain lighting think iPhone 12 or XS. It's not ugly but the colors are just so bland compared to the 16.  And it's a shame that Apple cannot seem to release at least 1 fun color or something bold on the Pro.  Like Pro people cannot have a bit of fun?  Its insane.   The white is also quite nice its actually like white not some creamy off white like the 15 pro max was, but like true Apple white.  The other colors are meh.  If you like Black that is closer to pure black or the Space Black MacBook Pro. 

Camera / Button: I dont really use my camera that much, but it's definitely top notch.  But so was the 15Pro Max so what are we really gaining here?  I feel like these have become more professional cameras and everything is like a side show.  That's fine for the pro photographers but I feel like they are missing people that do other things on their phones.  The button is meh.  It's cool to capture photos relatively quickly but it's positioned weird so your mileage may vary and the scroll thing on is too gimmicky to futz with for me anyway.  If you have a case on make sure you get one that supports it or you may not be able to access the button properly and it will drive you nuts. 

iOS 18:  Again it's OK, I feel like iOS is getting to be bloated.  The bottom bar is different in many apps and it drives me nuts particularly on the Max.  Even the new you can place icons anywhere is still half baked.  And the setup is a hot mess!  I dont know who tested that nightmare ugh but I recommend doing the encrypted backup to get started.  Phone to Phone is a joke this year.  The lack of multitasking on the Max is also a huge missed opportunity.  The screen is huge but you cannot do anything different from the smaller one?  Like what.  that just doesn't make sense.  

Battery:  Exceptional!  This thing lasts forever.  

Compared to iPhone 16 Pro:  I got the regular Pro first to see if the 6.3 would be good enough since I had a max for years but they are just so heavy I got sick of them.  I tried for a few days and it was lighter but still quite dense so the weight savings were not that great overall.  The max weighs a bit more but its spread over a larger area so feels less dense and therefore feels lighter.  Still they are both heavy.  The 16Pro is nice but the 6.3 is just still too small sadly.  Hopefully the 6.5 iPhone 17 is the goldilocks with hopefully 120MHz and nice colors.

Overall Its an iPhone and a decent one but for the price it should be better at this point.

Clean, simple, a beacon of technological achievmnt. I bought this for a family friend. He met my wife at church, and she introduced him to me so that I could do some web development for him. He was a business owner, a family man, proud & strong. Turns out he got lymphoma and needed a bone-marrow transplant. Needed to get chemo first, and they needed to see his response before moving forward. Bear in mind, he never told me any of this until it was too late. The chemo didn't take, the bone marrow was still in need of transplanting, and his family decided to disown him. Like, they wanted him to die right away so they could claim his assets. He bought this phone so he could live "off grid" and watch his Netflix movies in peace at the hospital, hoping his family could forgive him for a grievance or sin that he never shared with me & I could only guess at being. It took me minutes to setup, the quality was topnotch, and the value was fantastic. He ended up buying the phone with the touchscreen but for the brief moment of time that he had with this phone, and the subsequent brief moment of life that he had after the diagnosis, this phone was a source of joy for him. If you're still reading this, please setup your will & trust. For when you're in your darkest hour, if the only person by your side is someone's husband that would fix your wifi & setup your phone, whose wife you met in church will you crumble away, with your family praying you die as soon as possible to take all your assets, you know that somewhere along the way you took the wrong path. Peace and love to all those in the struggle.

This phone is one of the best values you can get in a flagship, especially if you're more of a power user. - Great hardware 
- Battery life is great
- Charging is extremely fast with a larger battery capacity as well
- Hasselband cameras allow for great shots
- Green Marble Finish (my favorite design of any phone thus far) :)
- Customizable and Unlockable (officially)
- Exceptional Value 

Cons:
- Battery life is a little lackluster COMPARED to reviews. This being said: It lasts a lot longer than other phones I've owned. It easily gives me over a day of idle with typically slightly over 8 hours of heavy use. I've seen where people get more than this but to be fair, I use a lot of heavy battery consumption apps.
- Battery might need a few learning cycles for calibration (use phone until it runs completely, charge it while off to 100%). This is kind of an annoyance but if you do this a couple times, you'll get better battery life. This teaches the phone how to best utilize battery life (you know how modern tech and ML goes)
- UI interface. While not awful, I do think the UI could be better. Not as clean as the Pixels, not as customizable as others (Xiaomi, Oppo, Samsung, etc)

Overall, there's nothing I really hate about this phone. The cons are just slight critiques rather than actual problems. Currently not a phone on the market that I would choose to use over this one. And like.. just look at the green marble colorway.. :)

A very, very solid choice in a phone.. To start with, I am slightly biased in this phone's favor anyway, as my previous phones of the last few years have also been Motorola so I bought the Edge Plus 2023 being mostly certain I'll like it and 'wanting' to like it -- and I LOVE IT.
There is no better choice in a smartphone today than this phone. It is a very, very, very solid choice in a phone even late into 2023, and it will easily be good to go for a few years before ever even needing to entertain the thought of upgrading to something else. The specs on this phone are flagship level, and it has years of updates to rely on.
While the cameras and the speed and the fat battery all the other stuff is really amazing, the display is my favorite feature of the phone, as the display is simply gorgeous when utilizing the full gambit of the phone's capabilities; i.e., setting the refresh rate to max 165, adjusting the colors to Saturated instead of Natural, and making use of the phone's ample amount of brightness nits to bump that brightness slider up and make everything look incredible. This display is so clear and bright and vivid and is just absolutely amazing. A phone's display is VERY important to me, and this display fully delivers.
In this price range, you may also be considering the Oneplus 11. That is a really nice phone as well and is impressive in its own right. It is competitive with the Edge Plus 2023 and is in the same league, but I do personally feel that the Moto ultimately 'edges' it out.
The S23 Ultra is of course the big baddie of modern Android smartphones, but I've had one of those also and you may think I'm exaggerating to say this, but I prefer the Edge Plus 2023 to the S23 Ultra. This may be an unpopular opinion but I just do not think Samsung phones are worth the extreme prices they cost. I couldn't care less about the stylus pen, and I couldn't care less about having a 200 mp camera. The S23 Ultra is just way too gimmicky. You're paying for a lot of really unnecessary stuff in that phone that you won't be using. I also dislike the Samsung software apps. I very greatly prefer Google apps.
So anyway, enough of the novel I'm writing. Suffice to say that I love the Motorola Edge Plus 2023 and whole heartedly endorse it. It is an incredible, incredible piece of technology.
Finally, a note or two on cases and screen protectors.
As for cases, Poetic has nice offerings that work well with this phone, though I recommend using only the Poetic case itself and not the optional built in screen protector which in my opinion sucks. Use a separate screen protector. On that note, curved screens are apparently here to stay, so get used to having to deal with flimsy TPU screen protectors, because tempered glass protectors are never going to work well on curved screens.
It takes some patience and more patience, and still a little more patience to learn how to apply these TPU screen protectors well and to understand that it takes a day or two after installation for any little bubbles and such to disappear. Do your research and be patient. You'll get it, maybe not right away, but you'll get it! Again, patience. Repeat that like a mantra. Patience. PATIENCE! (grasshopper)

The S-Pen screen recording features, like for screenshots and GIFs, are reintroduced as Galaxy AI features when using the OneUI version of Circle To Search. It works just as well as it did on the previous few generations of Samsung phones with OneUI.

I mean, idk what else to really say. The titanium frame is rigid, the battery life lasts as long as any other phone, and the volume is really good from the speakers. It'll be more than enough for you.

The Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra is a beast of a phone, but it's not a huge leap from last year's model. The camera system shines with a new 50MP ultrawide lens that nails sharp, vibrant shots, especially in low light, and the 200MP main camera is still a champ for detailed photos. Video recording gets a boost with 10-bit HDR for richer colors and an Audio Eraser tool to cut background noise—super handy for clean clips. The AI, powered by Galaxy AI and Google's Gemini, is a mixed bag. Features like Now Brief (a daily summary of your schedule and news) and voice-activated cross-app actions (like adding events to your calendar) are useful but sometimes glitchy or incomplete, like misidentifying locations or missing app integrations. The S Pen's AI sketching tools are cool for creatives, but overall, the AI feels more like a work in progress than a game-changer.

Display & Design
The QHD+ AMOLED screen is an absolute stunner: super bright, crisp, and easy to read even in direct sunlight when dialed up  . Rounded edges and flat titanium frame feel premium and refined, although it still looks very familiar to previous Ultra models—some might even call it boring  .

Performance & Software
Under the hood is the Snapdragon 8 Elite paired with 12 GB of RAM, offering smooth day-to-day use. I didn't experience any lag, and Galaxy AI feels genuinely helpful—for instance, using Gemini via long-pressing the side button is far more responsive than Bixby ever was  . One UI 7 on Android 15 runs cleanly and comes with bold new features like the “Now Brief” widget, vertical app drawer, and an improved Select tool—even if UI bugs still sneak in occasionally  .

Battery & Charging
The S25 Ultra retains a 5,000 mAh battery, but thanks to internal optimizations, I consistently got 1½ days of use on a charge—better than past Samsung flagships  . Charging is decent with 45 W wired speeds—70% in 30 minutes—but it doesn't match the sub‑40 min charge times seen in some rivals  .

Best Bang for your Buck Phone on The Market. I was generally shocked at just how nice the Google Pixel 7 phone is at the price this point. As someone who has been on iOS since smartphones came out, I was proud of how fast I was able to adapt to Android in just a matter of minutes. Having a Google email account already made setting up the Pixel 7 a breeze. Since I'm using this phone strictly as a work phone, and having all my contacts already tied to my Gmail made importing all my contacts super easy and convenient. This little phone packs a punch and goes toe to toe with my personal $1200 phone. Right out of the box you notice just how nice the display is and the snappiness of the 90Hrz screen refresh rate is when scrolling through texts and photos. The face unlock feature is sneakily one of greatest features, in that as soon as it sees your face, it will immediately unlock your phone without having to also swipe up, whereas coming from other phones this now seems like a waste of time to also have to swipe up. The camera is very nice, in that it takes amazing photos, Google has implemented some great tech here. I don't know how to exactly explain how it works but when focusing on the object you want to shoot, the object on screen doesnt look like the best quality on screen but once the photo is taken it upreses the photo and looks 10x better, truly some impressive tech. And having to ability to change setting like resolution right from the camera app and not having to go to the settings app, is nice quality of life addition, 
Another cool camera feature that I accidentally stumbled upon is the “Google Lens” feature, where if you take a picture of a product box it will then analyze the box and show you youtube videos of it or take you to where you can purchase the item directly. A really cool feature that I can see myself using a lot when it comes to things like price matching, finding an item in stock or watching a Youtube review on a product before buying it. Another one of my favorite little things about the haptic feedback when typing is that it almost feels like typing on a physical keyboard and I notice myself making a lot less typing errors with this keyboard than other phone keyboards. Also, I also highly recommend putting a case on this phone because of the glass back for protection and fingerprints just cover the back real easy.
So, overall you can’t go wrong with the Google Pixel 7, where you get a top end phone for a fraction of the price compared to the other phones on the market.

Acceptable, but not great. The Razr+ 2023 is a decent phone in some ways, but is overshadowed by what appears to be some quality control issues. I've now owned two of these phones, and while the second one is a little better than the first one, I'm still a bit disappointed. Maybe that's my own fault for having higher expectations for a flip phone of this style, or maybe it's due to Motorola's attempts at making an "affordable" flip phone. Either way, this phone leaves a bit to be desired.

In both cases, the middle part of the screen on the phone has obtained horizontal wear lines that have appeared in the phones screen protector overlay due to the motion of opening / closing the phone. This is highly distracting for me and really shouldn't be happening at all for a phone like this, especially given I've only had this particular phone for maybe 4 months now?

The hinge on the phone is extremely fragile, and you need to find a good case with hinge protection if you want the phone to last. Unfortunately there are hardly any good options for cases for this particular phone model that have hinge protection, and the ones that do seem to interfere with the limited outer screen protector options currently available for this phone model. So you can either get a case with hinge protection, or get a case that allows for the outer screen to be protected, but not necessarily both. This is likely due to this being a Motorola brand phone which doesn't seem nearly as popular in the market overall.

The screen size is tall, but fairly narrow in comparison to most other phones advertised at this size, so apps and movies seem a bit squished in comparison to other phone styles. Performance is decent but not noticeably better than other mid range Motorola phones (like the moto g power for example.) Battery doesn't even last a full day at this point either, which is a tad annoying (again, only had this four months or so.) Outer camera is good, selfie camera is ok.

All in all I guess I was expecting more than what I got, and I don't like owning a phone that I'm so constantly worried about possibly damaging in some way. Never had this worry with other non-flip style phones.

The Pixel is a Great Everyday Phone!. Google has had a long and tough road in the Android phone space since 2016 with the Pixel line.  The Pixel was the first Google phone where they took full control of the hardware and the software.  They’ve seen their market share only grow to about 5% total in the world, but have stuck with refining the Pixel, making improvements along the way, and trying to create a great phone for the everyday Android user.  And I believe this years Goole Pixel 9 is a very good representation of the growth and strides they’ve made over the years!  Let’s Dive Into the review!
Initial unboxing was straightforward and super simple.  Upon turning on the Pixel 9 it detected my OnePlus and asked if I wanted to transfer to the new phone using a QR code.  Moving all my data over was super seamless and took about 30-45 minutes total, but it even allowed me to transfer sims by using an esim with my new phone without having to call my provider!  Overall, just a very easy and stress-free experience!
First impressions were very positive. The phone feels great to hold in your hand, and has a nice weight and balance to it .  The screen has a fingerprint sensor that is very responsive to the touch and solid facial recognition as well.  The 120hz 6-inch Gorilla glass screen goes edge to edge and is plenty bright even out in broad daylight and after a week’s use has not shown any scratches on the screen without a glass protector.  128gb of storage and 12gigs of ram are standard, 256gb is the biggest storage size you can choose.  Theres 2 cameras, a 50MP Wide and a 48MP Ultrawide Camera that both are packed with a lot of cool features like Night Sight, which allows you to take Astrophotography style photos!  The 50 MP Wide has 4k/1080p Video capabilities and a host of video features like Dual exposure, Cinematic Blur and Pan, slo-mo up to 240fps and many others!  The 48 MP Ultrawide even doubles as a macro lens and can focus on items up to 2 cm away.   Battery comes in at 4700mAh, which lasts all day for me with normal usage and settings.  You can use an extreme battery setting that supposedly lets your phone last up to 100 hours, but I haven’t tested that fully.  The phone also features wireless charging and fast charging ability to 55% in 30 minutes with the right charger.  Features like SOS which allows you to contact emergency services without a signal, and Car Crash detection for those moments when you can’t dial are useful additions!  The Pixel 9 launched with Android 14 but will be the first phone to receive Android 15 and comes with seven years of OS, security, and Pixel Drop updates, making sure that the phone won’t become obsolete anytime soon!
One of the bigger focuses for the Pixel is Google’s first foray into A.I.  The Gemini is Google’s A.I assistant system that they have built into the OS to try and help with your everyday life.  I am still catching on to how to really utilize A.I more, but I am enjoying figuring out a new technology and how it can best work for me.  The other A.I. features they have built into the Cameras with settings like Add Me and Magic Editor are neat but take a little getting used to.  I will say that my first attempts at Add Me looked pretty fake.  The one feature that did work well was Best Take, which finds the best smile for each person and edits that into the photo.  Taking photos with my 2 year old son is hard and it actually did a good job capturing his best smile.  I believe all these features will get better as time goes on and updates are made!
Overall, the Google Pixel 9 is a very solid Android phone for the everyday smartphone user.  It has a lot to offer with a Gorilla Glass screen, great camera system, good battery life and with 7 years of updates will be a good phone for years to come.  It should seriously be considered if you’re looking for a new Android phone, at a solid price point, with a lot of useful features.  Google has made a really nice phone with the Pixel 9 and I hope its recognized and continues to gain market share.

Disappointing bugs from this indie company. I've been using a Samsung Galaxy S7 for years, and I wanted to see what the Pixel was like. I was thinking about getting the Pixel 6, but there were lots of reviews pointing out how buggy it was. The Pixel 7 seemed much improved, so I decided to try it out.

The main thing that pulled me toward the Pixel was the camera. 5x zoom optical zoom seems more practical than 10x. The pixel also seems to have excellent night/low light photos, which my older Galaxy didn't handle well. I haven't had a chance to test this much, but I expect the camera to do well.

Overall it took some getting used to navigating on the Pixel compared to my old Galaxy, but I've gotten used to it now. It feels pretty fluid and responsive. The extra screen size is nice, but this phone is huge compared to the S7. I think it's about a full inch longer on the diagonal. This is extremely noticeable with both the weight and the length. It's pretty difficult to use with one hand, but a textured case can help a lot. I have one with a groove in the middle of the back, and I can stabilize the both with one hand by placing a finger in that groove.

I miss some of the stock Samsung apps, namely the Clock and Memo apps. These apps were way more capable than what Google offers. I found another note app that should work. The Pixel Clock app is pretty limited in customizing alarms, so I may look for a replacement later there as well.

The main reason I give a low rating on this phone is I've already run into some buggy behavior. Recently, the camera refused to display anything on the screen, though it could still take photos. This seemed to go away after restarting the phone, but that was concerning.

My BIGGEST gripe with this phone is the brightness adjustments. It's so buggy... I think I have a 20% chance of being able to adjust the brightness on any given attempt. I saw posts online saying this was linked to using the smallest display setting on the phone. I haven't messed with that yet.

If Google ever releases a fix for this, I'll update from 2 stars to 4 stars. For Google's latest offering on their "Pro" model, I find this extremely irritating.

After a week I finally got my case. That problem solved. The camera lump I knew about at the purchase so I have to live with that. But the fingerprint reader is completely unacceptable. I changed my rating from 4 stars to 3 stars. I used the fingerprint reader on my 4a constantly. Without a screen protector and with screen sensitivity turned all the way up, I got an estimated 80% failure to read. After putting the screen protector on today I reinstalled my prints; both thumbs and both index fingers. I made sure the screen sensitivity was at the max. The phone allows 6 tries before switching to your PIN to open. I turned the lock screen on 24 times and used each finger 6 times until the PIN screen came up. So 6 print scans for each of 4 fingers, times 6 attempts for each before the PIN screen came up is 144 attempts. The phone was successful once. That is a 0.69% success rate. If you use the fingerprint scanner on your phone don't buy this one. And don't believe Google's baloney excuses like I did. My Pixel 4a worked great. I wasted $699 on this Pixel 6 / 256.

Great Design, Software, and Value!. The Pixel 7 Pro (and 7) is Google’s latest generation of the Pixel lineup. The Pixel 7 and 7 Pro offer Google’s 2nd generation in house processor, Tensor G2, with Titan M2 security coprocessor for enhanced protection. Tensor G2 has been enhanced vs the original chipset to offer better performance in every area but specifically in software optimization and machine learning. The design is also evolution rather than revolution. I have had hands on time with both the Pixel 7 Pro and the regular Pixel 7 so I will try to mention both but this review will focus mostly on the P7P (Pixel 7 Pro).
	 
Design:

	The design for the P7 has been revised vs the last generation. The camera bar is still proudly displayed across the back but instead of being glass, this time it is finished in aluminum. The two tone colors are gone (RIP) but the colors offered are still premium looking. The P7 gets matte aluminum vs the P7P polished/shiny aluminum. I prefer the matte finish on the regular P7. The buttons on the right of the P7P are moved downwards for easier reach (awesome!) and the curved front glass on the P7P is less curved. I prefer flat glass phones but the curve isn’t too intrusive but something to get used to. Both phones get Corning® Gorilla® Glass Victus™ glass front and back unlike the last generation where only the P6P had to front and back. The P6 only had it on the front where the back was a different glass.

Screen: 

	Both phones get brighter screens this year for better outdoor performance. The P7’s screen is .1” smaller than P6 but this is not easily noticeable just by looking at the device.

	The Pixel 7 features a 6.3-inch 60-90Hz AMOLED panel with FHD+ resolution stretching 1080 x 2400 pixels. This comes with a 20:9 aspect ratio, 416ppi pixel density, and an 84.9% screen-to-body ratio.

	The Pixel 7 Pro features a 6.7-inch adaptive 10-120Hz LTPO AMOLED panel with QHD+ resolution stretching 1440 x 3120 pixels. This comes with a 19.5:9 aspect ratio, 512ppi pixel density, and an 88.7% screen-to-body ratio.

	Both phones come with Corning Gorilla Glass Victus (front and back), support HDR10+ content and always-on display. The biggest difference is the curved display on the P7P and higher resolution/refresh rate. The higher resolution is a nice bonus for me as I have been using the Pixel 6 for a year. Like I have mentioned with the design, I would prefer a flat screen. 

	The P7P features a screen that supports up to 120hz refresh rate vs the 90hz found on the P6/P7. I have not noticed a huge difference here the quicker refresh rate should make scrolling more fluid. I have to say I have experienced bugs that seem to cause minor shudders in the scrolling that others online have experience too. I hope this gets resolved because it doesn’t seem to be at its full potential at all times. The optical fingerprint sensor returns with the addition of face unlock via the upgraded front camera. As with the P6, I still get failed finger print attempts on occasion which bugs me but it’s a relatively minor gripe. The software seems improved to do this less often but it’s likely due to the nature of the sensor itself being optical vs ultrasonic.
   
Android 13:

	The Pixel 7 series launch with Android 13 which is the latest version of Android. The P7 gets, at minimum, 3 years of software updates and 5 years of security updates. As far as I know this is the longest period of support for Android phones. This is why many owners enjoy using their Pixel’s for 3+ years. I have family who just upgraded from their P2 and P3 for the P7 due to great trade in offers. As long as the hardware holds up over time, it is nice to know Google will be there is support the phone for many years to come. UI changes are incrementally as with most versions of Android. If you would like a full tutorial of Android 13, I would recommend searching online otherwise it’s bloatware free, nearly stock Android.

	One minor gripe I have that I have experienced on the P6 with Android 13 as well is that the Always on Display time will freeze at random and not update to the correct time until the phone is unlocked. If you leave the phone on a table and don’t come back for a longer period, it may still be showing a time in the past.  

Battery Life:

	I have had outstanding battery life compared to my last device. The P7P features a 4926 mAh battery which is about the same as the P6P. The P7 battery is about 5.5% smaller than the P6.  The software optimization seems better on the P7’s than the P6’s before. I have easily been able to make it through a normal day with plenty of battery to spare. I have gotten between 3-4 hours of screen on time within my battery usage and I have no doubts many more is possible depending on the type of usage. I never seem to get what other press user get for battery life but conditions vary between users. I would say this phone can easily make it through a full, long day without issue. 

Speakers:

	The speakers are a little worse than the P6 from my experience. They lack a little bass that the P6 had. Still very loud and usable but the sound is not quite as good.
 
Cameras:

 	The main camera on the P7’s is a carryover from the P6 (I think). This is a 50MP (f/1.85) sensor that does Pixel binning to create a final 12.5MP image. The Ultra Wide is also a carryover at 12MP (f/2.2) with a FOV of 114 degrees. The Pro model gets a third, telephoto camera that is upgraded vs the previous P6P. This camera is a 48MP (f/3.5) with a 20.6 degree FOV and 5x optical zoom. 

	Google’s nifty camera tools such as Magic Eraser, Night Sight, and Super Res Zoom. One of the new features is Photo Unblur which will take a slightly blurry photo and use AI to unblur it. This works very well in most scenarios where there is a slight shake in the camera. I have been very happy with image quality of all camera on the P7. The ultra wide is the least clear of the three cameras and it’s still a little better than last year. Google software optimization is really what makes the photo shine. The P7 still features video shooting abilities of up to 4K at 60FPS. The main camera and telephoto feature Laser Autofocus and Optical (and Electronic) Image Stabilization. 10-bit HDR video has been added for better colors throughout.

	The front camera on both phones has been upgraded to a 10.8MP (f/2.2) sensor with 92.8 degree FOV. This camera supports face unlock with digital imagine processing as there is no infrared sensors on the front. This means it may get tricked or not be as accurate as others with infrared sensors. This camera also supports video up to 4K at 60FPS.  

Performance:

	The P7 and P7P feature Tensor G2 which is an updated version of Tensor. This is paired with 8GB of ram on the P7 and 12GB on the P7P. Google has improved just about every aspect of the chipset, albeit fairly mildly. Coming from the P6, I have not noticed any major improvements but Google claims the upgrades allow for “more advanced machine learning… offering a 60% faster, and 20% more efficient performance”. This excels in the area of speech recognition and any AI actions. The software optimization is really where Google can get the maximum performance behind the hardware. This is an advantage as well as a detriment because bugs can (and likely will) get introduced which hinder the performance of the phones. My hope is that Google does a better job of software updates vs the P6 series.

Verdict:
 
	The Pixel 7 Pro has been amazing to use and feels like a true upgrade vs the Pixel 6. The enhanced performance leaves a little headroom for upgrades, the software seems less buggy, and the design is refined for better aesthetics. Google addressed most areas where the P6 fell a little short and added new features to keep the phone relevant. The absolute best part? The price is unchanged from the P6 series! This easily makes the P7 one of the best values in the market. The P7P on the other hand is a little harder to justify but I believe still offers a solid deal if you need the third camera, larger screen, or just want the best specs out of the Pixel series.

I hate having the power button and volume buttons on the same side, and being on the same side, I hate having the power button above the volume rocker.
